claim: A rapid slope failure involving glacier ice generated a far-traveled debris flow and flood.
The source was not yet resolved between a landslide incorporating glacier ice and collapse of glacier ice itself.
No event-specific climate attribution can yet be assigned from the provisional agency reconstruction.
A rock and glacier-ice avalanche transformed into a highly mobile debris flow; no glacial-lake outburst was required.
Spontaneous threshold failure is the most conservative classification; preceding snowfall and a temperature anomaly are plausible but unproven final perturbations.
Long-term warming may have perturbed permafrost bedrock and promoted glacier decline and meltwater infiltration, but formal anthropogenic event attribution was not performed.

A rockslide struck and entrained a gully glacier before entering the fjord and generating a tsunami and long-lived seiche.
No meteorological or other proximate trigger was demonstrated for 16 September 2023.
Multidecadal glacier thinning likely debuttressed the unstable toe; this is a mechanistic climate link rather than formal event attribution, and site-specific permafrost thaw was not shown.
The commonly used 2024 label is the paper's publication year; the landslide occurred on 16 September 2023.
A smaller rock or ice avalanche in the same gully likely generated the 11 October tsunami and week-long signal, but no new scar was resolved.
A bedrock landslide entered the fjord beside South Sawyer Glacier and generated a tsunami and a seiche detected globally for as long as 36 hours.
Several days of rain were not extreme; the study did not isolate a unique immediate trigger.
Anthropogenic warming drove glacier thinning and retreat that exposed and removed support from the slope; mapped and modeled permafrost is unlikely at the site.
Several days of microseismicity accelerated in rate and magnitude until about one hour before failure.
The Tracy Arm concern and the large 2025 Alaska landslide refer to the same occurred event; they should not be counted twice.
Barry Arm is a monitored moving slope rather than an occurred catastrophic failure.
Slope acceleration covaried with glacier retreat; the authors infer that glacier debuttressing was likely the main cause of 2010--2017 instability.
A possible precipitation response in 2017 was tenuous and did not persist in later observations.
